findings.question: q-chemistry-solutions-0008
findings.quote: Many solids become less soluble when heated, with exceptions.
findings.problem: The stem asks for an accurate statement, but “many” does not mean “most” or “the usual trend.” Many solids can become more soluble while many others become less soluble. The lesson explicitly gives cerium(III) sulfate as a solid that becomes less soluble when heated. The revised distractor describes a real class of solids rather than denying the common trend, so it is defensible alongside the key.
findings.fix: Ask for the usual trend for solids in water, and make all choices parallel statements of competing usual trends.

findings.question: q-chemistry-solutions-0019
findings.quote: This invents a turning point in the trend. Warmer liquids hold less gas at each step. Check the lesson's gas-solubility behavior.
findings.problem: “Warmer liquids hold less gas at each step” turns the common trend into an absolute. For example, helium solubility in water can increase with warming above its solubility minimum. The lesson correctly says gas solubility usually falls. The note must explain why this is not the common trend without denying real exceptions.
findings.fix: Say that a rise followed by a fall is not the common trend; liquids usually hold less dissolved gas as they warm at fixed gas pressure.

findings.question: q-chemistry-solutions-0019
findings.quote: Dissolved gases commonly become less soluble as the liquid warms at fixed gas partial pressure. The equilibrium concentration therefore commonly decreases.
findings.problem: “Gas partial pressure” and “equilibrium concentration” repeat the stem in technical language without explaining it for a Grade 5 reader. A learner who does not know those terms gets no plain account of what decreases.
findings.fix: Say: “When the pressure of the gas above the liquid stays the same, a warmer liquid usually holds less dissolved gas.”
